paragraphs.text: Come, let us once more offer you the first-fruits of the gospel streams; come, let us draw with you from the clear, pure current, obeying the prophet who says, "Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation." The springs are many, but salvation is one. There is one spring of all good things, our Lord Jesus Christ, who has rained down all knowledge and all wisdom. And I am amazed that the Jews are astonished that he knows letters without having studied. For this is what was just read to us: when the Savior was setting forth his divine teaching, the Jews were amazed. "How," they say, "does this man know letters, when he has never studied?" They look for letters from the spring of the Word, or rather from God the Word. They demand letters from Christ, who brought in the law, who supplied prophecy, from whom comes all knowledge and reason and law and purpose and reflection. For "all wisdom is from the Lord." They look for letters from the Word, from whom all the prophets drew, and whom all the theologians received into the cisterns of their own souls. Moses received him; from this spring the prophets drew; from this spring all the apostles received. And John bears witness, saying, "From his fullness we have all received." Do you demand letters from God, as though letters had made the Word, rather than the Word having invented the art of letters? Did letters make the Word? No, the Word discovered the nature of letters. Just as the arts did not give birth to their materials, but the materials furnished the arts with their starting point, so letters did not make the Word; the Word discovered the science of letters. Letters do not come first and the Word second; the Word comes first, and letters come from it. Everything that comes from God goes before, and then what belongs to human skill follows. The eye did not make the things that are seen; the eye discerns the nature of what is seen. The arts did not give us hands; hands produced the arts. Running did not fashion feet; feet showed what running is. So too letters did not reveal the Word; the Word invented the science of letters. Why then do you look for secondary things from the spring of the primary ones? Because "he knows letters without having studied." You are not amazed that he raises the dead, yet you are struck by his knowing letters without having studied, which is something possible to nature. For those who first discovered letters did not learn them from someone else when they discovered them, and the discoverers of letters were human beings. But raising the dead surpasses human nature. Do you overlook the great things and quibble over the small? Christ, then, is the spring of all wisdom and all knowledge. Nothing escapes him. For he is the discoverer of all things. I mean this not as though another made them and he merely devised them, but because he himself is both the maker of wisdom and the discoverer of all that is contemplated in wisdom. Nothing past, nothing present, nothing future escapes him, for he is the spring of all things.

"If, then," says the heretic (for tares spring up among the wheat), "if, then, he is the spring of wisdom and knowledge, how can he say of that day, that is, of the consummation, when the resurrection of the dead and the coming of the Savior will take place, that no one knows it, neither the angels nor the Son, but only the Father? How then is he a spring of wisdom if he does not know the future?" I would rather you did not twist the word with malicious cunning or wind yourself up in verbal convolutions, but let yourself be carried along by the straightness of the doctrines. Why do you say, "If he is the spring and treasury of wisdom, how can he not know?" I know that the saying is deep, but we will come to it briefly. One must aim not at the full force of the subject but at the capacity of the hearers. For the apostle says of Christ, "We are led into the knowledge of the mysteries of God the Father and of Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden." If all things are in him, nothing escapes him. What then does the heretic say about the Savior's statement, "No one knows, not even the Son, but only the Father"? Let the heretic be asked: which is greater, the day or the Father? Does the one who knows the Father not know the day? "No one knows the Father except the Son." He has found the Father, then. Does he know the spring of knowledge and yet not know the day? "But it is possible," he says, "to know the Father and yet not know what is in the Father." If there is something in the Father hidden from the Son, then there is something in the Son hidden from the Father. How so? The Master of all has himself laid down the rule: "As the Father knows me, so I know the Father." But when he speaks about human beings, he says, "I know my own and am known by my own." Between Father and Son there is no inequality of knowledge. Where nature is unequal, knowledge too is unequal. A human being can know God, but not what is in God. We all know the Father, but not as the Son does. "That they may know you, the only true God." We all know him, but not as he does. For the fruit recognizes the root in one way, the root expresses the fruit in another, and those who harvest the fruit partake of it in yet another. But here he has stated a clear and unmistakable equality of knowledge: "As the Father knows me, I know the Father." If there is something in the Son hidden from the Father, there is something in the Father hidden from the Son. Are you not ashamed even of that saying, heretic, by which you rob the Son of knowledge? From another angle, by your reckoning, you make the Holy Spirit, whom you deny, greater than the Son. For Paul says of the Holy Spirit, "The Holy Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." The Holy Spirit knows the depths, and the Son does not know the day? "If, then, he knows," he says, "why did he say, 'I do not know'?" It has been shown, both by the course of reasoning and by the testimony of the Scriptures, that he is the spring of knowledge and wisdom. Why, then, does he deny what he has, and say that he himself lacks the knowledge that springs from him? For he said that no one knows the day. We must, brothers, search out the Savior's purpose and ask what he is saying, about what, to whom, and when. One must not simply put words on the rack and scrutinize little phrases, but aim at the force of the meaning. For not everything the Savior says does he say as befits his own dignity; much of it he says to suit our weakness. He speaks one way to believers and another way to unbelievers. I know that I have already set out this idea among you, but nothing prevents us from traveling along the same line of thought and showing that the facts prove it true. The discourse was addressed to the Jews, Jews who were as far removed from the height of the Godhead as earth is separated from heaven, as God said: "As far as heaven is from the earth, so far are my ways from your ways and my counsels from your counsels." He was speaking, then, to unbelievers. And since they took him for some rival to God, campaigning against divine knowledge and opposed to the law of Moses, he everywhere conceals his own rank and refers everything to the Father's dignity, to show that the Jews were not contradicting him but fighting against the Father. With the Jews he often adapts his words to their own dispositions. This is not because the divine Word changes along with our characters, but because, like a physician, he applies remedies suited to the wounds, since he was dealing with Jews who had denied not only his Godhead but even his humanity. Consider how far they were from imagining a Son of God, when they did not even suppose the Lord to be a human being. For they said, "He has a demon," and took the Son of God for one possessed. Since, then, he saw the Jews contradicting him, and his own disciples, being human, prying into the future... For people always love to lay hold of what is coming and to know the future in advance. Indeed, even in ordinary life, if someone learns a day early what everyone will learn a day later, he is delighted, as though he had found something great and had received the knowledge of all things. People love, then, to search into the future. So the Savior saw this longing at its height in the apostles, and their passion for knowledge of the future boiling over, and he denies what he has, in order to check their untimely desire. "When will you restore the kingdom to Israel?" Then, curbing the human rashness that wants to lay hold of the future and pry into the things of God, he says, "It is not for you to know times or seasons." The measure of that knowledge exceeds human nature. Do not pry into the future before it happens; simply wait and believe in what is to come. Prepare yourself for the coming of the Judge who is to come. Concern yourself there, not to learn when the day will be, but to learn what kind of day will meet you. That is why the prophet, rebuking and silencing those who were curious about this day and kept saying, "When does the judgment come? When the resurrection?", said, "Woe to those who seek the day of the Lord! Why do you want this day of the Lord?" That is: why are you eager to see the day of the Lord? "The day of the Lord is appointed to be bitter and harsh, a mighty day of wrath, that day, a day of affliction and distress." He set fear before them to check their rashness. Since, then, they longed to know future things that exceed the human order, the Savior said, "It is not for you to know times or seasons." But so that he would not be thought to withhold the knowledge out of envy, he includes himself among those who do not know, to console human ignorance. "Not even the angels know," he says. Why do you fancy yourselves above the angels? "Not even the Son knows." Why do you fancy yourself above me? When you hear "Son," divide the matter in your mind. For "Son" is said in common of both the Godhead and the humanity. And so that you may learn that Scripture calls both the Savior's flesh and the economy "Son," it says elsewhere, "And the blood of Jesus his Son will cleanse us from all sin." Blood is not Godhead but humanity. So it calls the humanity "Son" as well. And when we say, "The Son of God suffered," we acknowledge what is capable of suffering and what is beyond suffering. When we say that the only-begotten Son of God was crucified, we distinguish what is beyond suffering and set apart what is capable of suffering. Among us human beings too there are expressions in use that apply to the whole human person but are divided by the mind's reflection. If we say that so-and-so has died, we understand what has died, the body, and what is immortal, the soul. And just because the term "death" is applied to the whole name, we do not say that the whole person has perished. Nor is it at all necessary to say, "This man's body has died." The name receives the common designation of death, but reason divides the designation into what has died and what has not. So the Savior too pronounces death in common terms of the saints, saying, "They will hand you over to councils, and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, and they will kill you." He pronounced it in common terms, but he himself divided it by his own teaching: "Do not fear," he says, "those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." The Savior does the same in the other case too. For just so here, though he has knowledge of all things, he says, "No one knows the day, not even the Son," meaning "not even I," with respect to the visible form. For the Son in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden is not ignorant. He who knows the Father as he is known by the Father is not ignorant. Here, then, is your solution: the name "Son" is used both for the dignity of the Godhead and for the form taken in the economy. So he is ignorant according to the form of his humanity, he who knows all things by the power of his Godhead.

It is the voice of the same one: "If I bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true." It is the teaching of the same one: "Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true." If it is true, how is it not true? The words conflict, but the meanings agree. Jesus went up into the temple and taught. The builder of the temple, the master of its worship, went up into the temple. He spoke in the temple so that the prophecy might be fulfilled which says: "And suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his own temple, and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire." He calls him both Lord and messenger. O divine mysteries! O glorious and prophetic initiation! "Suddenly he will come to his own temple." It is the temple of God. And he says that the temple is his, so that no one should think that the lordship of the Father belongs to one and the kingdom of the Son to another. The temple of the Father, which Solomon dedicated to God, is the very temple that the prophet calls the Savior's: "Suddenly the Lord will come to his own temple." Whenever, then, it is the temple of the Father, it is the temple of the Son; whenever it is the temple of the Son, it is the temple of the Father. That is why the Savior himself, when he drives the Jews out with a whip he had made of cords, says: "Take these things out of here, and do not make my Father's house a house of trade." And the same one again: "Take these things out of here, for my house shall be called a house of prayer." The house of my Father, and my house. And elsewhere the evangelist says: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." He is speaking of the Jews. For the Jews were his own, since he himself had enlightened them through the law and guided them through the prophets. And among the Jews were the Savior's own things. For when his mother went about looking for him and said, "Child, what have you done to us? We have been going around looking for you," he answers: "Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?" So he went up into the temple and taught, and another prophecy was fulfilled: "I myself who speak am here." He taught, and the teaching did no insult to his dignity; he was a teacher out of his love for humankind. When you hear that he taught, do not think that he was just one of the other teachers. And if the words "he taught" scandalize you, then when you hear someone say, "Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your statutes," you fail to recognize his dignity and do not marvel at his teaching. Jesus went up into the temple. Nowhere do you find him going down. He was going up from Jericho to Jerusalem; he went up onto the mountain. For where God is, there is ascent. "Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; your ascents are in his heart." Where there is virtue, there is ascent; where there is vice, descent. "Rescue me from those who go down into the pit." The Jews marveled: how does this man know letters when he has never studied? And "this man" is a word of arrogance, an announcement of contempt, a pose of malice. "How does this man...?" You say it to insult him, O Jew: "How does this man...?" But I take it up to glorify him. For one can say "this" with insult, and one can say "this" with glory. You say insultingly, "How does this man know?" But I say with Moses: "This is my God, and I will glorify him." He exposes the unbelief of the Jews; he publicly brands the disobedience of the people; he shows himself to be the fount of wisdom and the fount of all knowledge, and says: "My teaching is not mine, but the Father's who sent me." Everywhere he shows that those who did not receive the one they doubted are fighting against the God they acknowledged. Since God was believed among them, while Jesus was doubted among them, he hides his own dignity and puts forward the Father's authority, showing that whoever fights against Christ fights against God. But do you think the matter is mere irony and a contrivance of words rather than a demonstration from facts? Then take the proof from the facts themselves. According to your account, O Jew, you who despise Christ and disparage the Savior's deeds, this man is not of God and does not keep the law, but fights against piety, as the impious say. And you, by your own reckoning, champion the law, contend for the divine word, avenge God, and think yourself pious, repelling the glory of Christ while guarding the kingdom of the law. Let us see from the facts, then, how God casts his vote, by your judgment and by ours. According to your account, you are defending God and fighting against some rival of God who does not keep the law but dissolves God's ordinances. Let us see how God regards those who lay claim to the law and those who follow the one who opposes the law. I speak from common affairs. If a city receives a tyrant, it is in danger, even if it does not share his views; and since it received the tyrant at all, it shares in the dangers. But if a city shuts out a tyrant, it is thought worthy of admiration and receives rewards from the king, because in a time of danger it set up trophies, kept its resolve secure, and did not receive another tyrant in place of the king. This, O Jew, is what you did, according to your account. When the tyrant came, as your impiety has it, opposing the law of Moses, you did not receive him but sent him away, guarding the kingdom for God unharmed. The church of the Savior opened her gates, to a tyrant according to you, but according to her, to the King of glory. Let us see how the true one has voted concerning those who did not receive the king. One city did not receive him, and it has been leveled to the ground: Jerusalem. This one city shut its doors to the King of glory, and for not receiving the "tyrant" it lies leveled. The churches of God everywhere, having received salvation, flourish and thrive and are raised to an honor above the world. And again, consider it from the opposite side. While a tyrant lives, his friends who showed their loyalty in time of need are held in honor, and his enemies are in danger. But when the tyrant dies, his friends are in danger and his enemies speak freely. Let us see, then, after the Savior's end, after his departure from this age to the Father, after what you consider his death and what I believe to be his resurrection, let us see what happened after the end. If the enemies of the king, that is, the enemies of this "tyrant," are held in honor, then he is truly a tyrant. But if his enemies are in shame and exile, while his friends have boldness and glory, then, if you are not persuaded by words, be put to shame by the facts: see how God exalted the kingdom of Christ, and how he brought down those who rejected his kingdom. God could have destroyed them for denying the Son. He could have killed the enemies of the king, who thought the King of glory a tyrant. But he did not destroy them; he scattered them. If he had destroyed them, they would have had a defense: "If you had allowed us to remain on the earth, we would have been put to shame by the facts; if we had seen the earth believe, we too would have turned along with the whole world." The enemies could have said: "We saw him with twelve men and despised him as someone of no account. If we had seen him worshiped by kings, we would have bowed to the yoke of piety without objection. Why did you act first and take away our repentance, forestalling our correction with punishment?" For this reason, so that no one might say, "We knew him crucified, but we never saw him worshiped," he does not destroy them but scatters them. Their prophet David foresaw this and urged it: "Do not kill them, lest they forget your law; scatter them by your power." See them before the doors of Christ, selling handkerchiefs and aprons. He set them at the doors so that they might become witnesses of those who worship. See them standing at the gateways of the church like the brothers of Joseph. Consider that, just like Joseph's brothers, who on seeing their brother's dignity did not dare to approach him as one of their own but were afraid because of his dignity, so you see them trembling at the dignity of the church, which she received from God, from the Master and Savior of all. See them humbled and cowering as they see the crucified one in glory. Consider the passion, and consider the glory. The hours of the cross were three, from the sixth to the ninth; the time of the glory is ages of ages and is never used up. See how the insult passed like a shadow. See how the truth of the glory has flowered. From the sixth hour to the ninth, the insult; from age to ages, the glory, and the praise of Christ is not exhausted, his doxology is not spent. All pour out their voices, prophets and evangelists and shepherds, bishops and teachers, yet they can never exhaust the ocean of the Godhead. And just as the sea, receiving rivers, is not covered by the rivers but covers their streams, so all who speak of the glory of Christ are covered by the glory and do not cover the glory. Fearful is the daring of those who fight against God, but glorious is the honor of the one who was insulted for the sake of the dispensation, yet glorified for his divine dignity. Consider that, though the insult lasted three hours, ages of ages do not fill up the glory of God. Consider also the place of the cross. Did the spot where the wood stood measure even a single span around? The socket of the cross was the size of a foot. Consider the measure of the insult, and consider the regions under heaven, that the whole earth was filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas. The Jews stood around the cross laughing at the passion, or rather being laughed at by the passion. They saw the crucified one and did not recognize the glorified one. That is why the prophet Zechariah said: "Then the Lord God will come, and there will be great mourning in Jerusalem. For they will look upon him whom they pierced," that is, whom they fastened with nails. And he did not say, "They will look at him they pierced," but "upon that into which they pierced." What does "that into which" mean? It was the cross into which they pierced. Before the coming of the Savior, like a royal standard, what in common usage is called the signum, the cross runs ahead of Christ's coming, glorified by the angels. The cross will appear over the earth, overshadowing the sun and dimming the moon, as the Savior said: "Then the sign of the Son of God will appear in heaven." And so that the word of Zechariah might be fulfilled, the Savior took the very phrase and brought it to its fulfillment: "And then they will look upon him whom they pierced." The sign of the Son of God will be seen in heaven, and the tribes will mourn: "The tribe of the house of David by itself, and their women by themselves; the tribe of the house of Nathan by itself, and their women by themselves." Why then did he not give the name of a tribe, but a royal name? Why does the tribe of David mourn? For it was not called the tribe of David but the tribe of Judah. It is because those who were close in fleshly kinship to the one descended from David according to the flesh failed to recognize the dignity of his Godhead. So the calamity strikes first those who were close to him in kinship but far removed from him in their way of life. "The tribe of the house of Nathan." Who is Nathan? There was a prophet, and there was also a son of David. For Nathan the prophet, who rebuked David about his sin, is one person, and the Nathan descended from David is another. Read the accounts of the sons of David and you will find one of his children called Nathan. Luke the evangelist, tracing the line of succession down to Mary, also brings Joseph down through Nathan. See, the matter is deep and needs a careful mind. Read the Gospels, as the Savior said: "Search the Scriptures." He did not say "Read," but "Search." For bare reading does not produce knowledge; it is careful understanding that brings to light what is sought.

So the sign of the Son of God will be seen in heaven. It will be seen bearing the shape of the wood, but flashing out rays of light. And when the cross appears, the sun will be hidden, not blotted out but veiled by the surpassing greatness of the glory. The moon too will be hidden; the stars will be concealed, or rather they will fall, as it is written: "The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; the stars will fall from heaven." And then that fearful and glorious sign will be displayed, while the Jews look on and those who glorify it stand all around. Then each of the righteous will answer the unrighteous. Then Isaiah will say to us: "Behold our God, in whom we hoped, and we rejoiced." Then the cross, appearing, will expose the daring of the ungodly and confirm the church. Then those who spoke against him will be made to answer [?], and those who obeyed will be glorified. Then all creation will worship the Son of God, both the ranks of those who disbelieved and the ranks of those who believed, but the one with boldness, the other with shame. For in royal images the glory of the guards attending the king is depicted, together with the barbarian peoples subjected to the king. The barbarian bows down below, and the king's own countryman bows down too; yet the countryman stands with boldness, glorifying his king, while the barbarian, bound in fetters under his feet, worships the king but receives no reward for his worship. For it was not his will that brought him, but compulsion that bound him. And the upper row is of those who worship, the lower row of those who are prostrate. For to worship is one thing, and to fall prostrate another. So too, at the coming of the great King, the ranks of the believers will appear in the image of glory, singing hymns and giving glory with boldness alongside the ranks of the angels. And the ranks of the unbelievers will also appear, cast down under the feet of the great King. The one group will be set free by their boldness, the other bound by compulsion. For since the faithful were already bound by their longing, they need no chains; their longing is their bond. But those whom longing has not bound, compulsion often binds. And the faithful are brought before the King of glory with boldness: the faithful with boldness, while the inglorious, who spoke against the word of truth, will come forward bound in iron manacles. The one group will stand among the ranks of the worshipers on high, the other among the ranks of the prostrate in the depths. For just as in the images the band containing the worshipers is higher, and the band bearing the barbarians lower, so too in the kingdom of Christ the ranks of the believers must appear higher, and those of the prostrate low upon the ground and earthly. That is why the psalm, distinguishing those who worship from those who fall prostrate, says: "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him, for the kingdom is the Lord's, and he rules over the nations." There it showed the rank of those who worship. Then, regarding those who fall prostrate, it added: "Before him shall fall down all who go down to the earth." And how is the rank of the faithful higher? Because the faithful will not stand on the earth, but in the air, as assessors and fellow guards of the greatest King. For the throne of God is not set up on the earth; rather, the earth is the footstool of his feet. So all who are judged are below, while the judge and the judge's friends are above. That is why the apostle, wishing to show that the faithful will not stand on the earth but will be lifted up into the air, says: "And we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord."

These things came to my mind because of the audacity of those who fight against God, who dared to say, "He has a demon." Let us say with David: "How great is the abundance of your goodness, O Lord!" They say such things and dare such things against you, and you do not punish these enemies of God? Do you not destroy them with a single nod, destroy them with a word of command? Could you not even threaten them? Was it not of you that the prophet said, "He rebukes the sea and dries it up"? So fiercely do they fight against God, so fiercely do they blaspheme. But the Savior answers: "I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world." That is why David too, calling on him to come not to judge, as at the second coming, but to save, said: "You who are enthroned upon the cherubim, shine forth; stir up your might and come to save us", and not to judge. The first coming is for salvation, the second for judgment. If you are willing, you have come to know him as Savior; if you disobey, you have come to know him as Judge. Make yourself the King's friend beforehand.

Let us learn from everyday affairs. Do you not know people who leap and rejoice when some of their friends attain rank and promotion? Does not everyone rejoice when he sees someone he once knew advanced to office, and hope from then on to reap the fruits of the friendship? But people often prove false and change their friendships, and once in office they are friends no longer. Christ, however, does not hide the truth. Become his friend, and you will be his friend for ever. For often, brothers, rank has puffed a man up, changed his mind, altered his disposition, and he seems a different man from the one he was. Indeed, God, knowing that rank would change Saul, says of him: "I have anointed you lord; and they will make requests of you and give you rule, and you will receive from them. And when these signs come upon you, you will be turned into another man." For power and dignity will change you. Not that they change everyone: they do not alter the faithful man, but they expose the unsound one. That is why Scripture says to the faithful man: "If you are made a ruler, be like one of them yourself." If, then, friendship here has often proved false, though it often proves true as well, the friendship of Christ never fails. When you see him in glory, he will not disown you who worshiped him on earth; rather, just as he receives you into his friendship today, so he will call you then too and acknowledge the friendship: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father."

Here, often, even if you do someone a favor, he conceals that first kindness. He does not want to appear inferior to his benefactor, so he repays your friendship but hides your kindness. The Savior, however, both acknowledges the friendship and does not hide the kindness: "For I was hungry and you gave me food to eat," and so on. So the Savior shines in his friendship and shines in his kindness. He does not disown your earlier friendship; he acknowledges your disposition, proclaims your longing, crowns your purpose. Let us, then, have him as our benefactor and not as our judge. He is a judge, and a judge of truth. But you, act beforehand: make him your friend and not your judge, and win him over with your pleading. Have you not seen how people treat worldly rulers, how they run about and talk to those close to them? But here it is a matter of outward show; there it is a matter of intercession. Act beforehand: speak with the martyrs, converse with the apostles: "I beg you, prepare my Judge for me. May he be merciful to me at the time of judgment, when my deeds are examined. Persuade him; you are able to win him over. I know that he respects you. I have no confidence to speak; you speak to the King." But the apostles and martyrs will answer you: "Do you not know our God? He shows mercy freely, but he also wants to receive something from us. Give to the poor, and he himself will acknowledge your kindness in their place. Give into the hands of the poor, and, as one who has entrusted it to the hands of a faithful man, you will receive the reward. Give to Christ, who receives not out of greed but distributes to the poor out of love for humankind."

Does God, then, accept money? Not for himself, but for himself through the poor; not selling justice, but setting right our failings through repentance. For he does not take money in order to sell justice and condemn someone else unjustly, but in order to set you, the condemned, free through your giving, as Daniel said: "Redeem your sins by almsgiving, and your iniquities by compassion for the poor." Offer money in exchange for your soul, for "a man's own wealth is the ransom of his life."

I say these things in keeping with the dignity of Christ, our great Lord and Master, whom the whole world under heaven receives, of whom the church is now counted worthy, and of whom the synagogue alone is deprived. For it has been scattered. Its name is empty. It is something else: a "mutilation", for it is cut to pieces by unbelief. He calls the synagogue "the mutilation", as Paul also says: "Beware of the mutilation. For we are the circumcision." That is why those who called the Savior demon-possessed are cut off from glory, while those who confessed him as King were filled with glory.

I will tell one figure drawn from ancient history and then end my sermon. Once there was Gideon, a righteous man to whom the Scriptures bear witness, whom Paul too placed in the ranks of the righteous when he spoke of Gideon, Samson and Jephthah. This man, raised in all righteousness and having adorned his life with virtues, at a time of war and distress took some ears of grain from a certain place and was beating them out in a winepress, to provide himself some relief in his need. An angel stood beside him and said: "Be strong and courageous. The Lord is with you." For hunger does not dull righteousness; rather, virtue tested by afflictions shows itself the more brilliant. "The Lord is with you; peace be with you." And Gideon says: "If the Lord is with us, why have these evils come upon us?" He was not contradicting God, but speaking as one who considered himself unworthy of God, as if to say: "If we were worthy of God, these things would not have overtaken us." Unbelievers, who believe in word but fight against it in their thoughts, often say: "Where is the God of the Christians? Why did he not listen to the monks? Where do the wars come from? Where does the turmoil come from?" This man did not speak like that; he said: "If the Lord were with us, why have these evils come upon us?" Is he not among us, then? No, for we are not worthy of him.

The angel says: "The Lord is with you. God has given the victory into your hand; go out to war." Gideon says: "By this I will know that the Lord is with me, if he gives me a true sign. Look," he says, "I am laying down this fleece of wool. If God sends rain on this fleece and does not send rain on all the ground, I will know that God is with me." See the sign, and the request for a strange gift. He laid down the fleece. During the night God, by a divine rule and a reason beyond our grasp, brought the rain down on the fleece alone, and all the ground was dry. And Gideon, it says, took the fleece early, at daybreak, wrung it out, and a basin full of water was found. Then Gideon said again: "By this I will know that the Lord is with me, if he performs the sign I want. I am laying down this fleece, and if he sends rain on all the ground but does not send rain on this fleece, then I will know that the Lord is with me." Was the first sign not enough for you, that you ask for a second? Have you not read, "You shall not put the Lord your God to the test"? "I did not ask for two signs," he says; "I asked for one. The two are a single sign." That is why he said, "if the Lord gives me a true sign", meaning a figure standing for the truth that was to come. Then he laid down the fleece a second time, and rain came down on all the ground while the fleece stayed dry. After this trial he took courage for the war and defeated his enemies.

We must explain the riddle of the rain briefly. This fleece signified the Savior's first coming and his second. For the first coming reached Jerusalem alone, and the whole earth did not receive it. Just as the fleece is nothing compared with the whole earth, so too Jerusalem is nothing, a pitiful thing, compared with all the nations. That is why he said, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel", to that one nation alone. But since the grace of the Lord afterwards passed on, and the synagogue and that people were going to reject it while the whole earth was going to receive it, the figure foreshadowed this in the second sign. Just as at first the fleece alone was rained on while the ground was dry, and afterwards the ground was rained on while the fleece stayed dry, so at first the nation that was watered did not share its true religion with all the nations; but when all the nations received the blessing, Israel remained dry.

But so that this interpretation may not be thought something woven together from human reasoning and invention, I must bring forward the testimony of prophecy in its support. David, prophesying about the Savior, says: "O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son; he will judge your people with righteousness, and your poor with justice." And a little further on he says: "His name endures before the sun, and before the moon for generations of generations." Then, pointing to his coming, he says: "He will come down like rain upon a fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth." And immediately after: "And he will have dominion from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the inhabited world."

May we, then, watered together with all the earth, bear fruit, through the prayers and intercessions of our father and teacher, who is able to set his seal both on our words and on your longing, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and might, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
